newsitem.title: UK: Anti-windfall tax noises sound familiar to banks.
newsitem.headline: Anti-windfall tax noises sound familiar to banks.

text.p: Arguments against the new British Labour government's proposed windfall tax will sound familiar to those with memories stretching back to 1981 when, ironically, it was a Conservative administration that came up with the idea of taxing excessive profits.

Then, Britain's retail banks were the victims and senior bankers said on Friday that the words "retrospective" and "arbitrary", which are being used to criticise Chancellor Gordon Brown's proposal, were also in common usage in the early eighties.
"Nobody liked it, but it was very difficult to argue against it," said one banking source. "The government had to promise that it was a one-off thing."
Senior bankers can still remember the zeal with which Margaret Thatcher's government, with Geoffrey (now Lord) Howe in charge at the Treasury, set about killing inflation.

Interest rates went through the roof, with clearing bank base rates reaching a peak of 17 percent in November 1979 and remaining firmly in double figures throughout 1980. Base rate stands at 6-1/4 percent now after a recent 1/4 point rise.
The idea for the tax is usually attributed to then Financial Secretary to the Treasury Nigel Lawson, who later became Chancellor and is now Lord Lawson.

Banks paid 2-1/2 percent of their sterling deposits which added up to around 355 million pounds ($583 million) -- well over a billion pounds at today's prices -- with Barclays paying 94 million pounds and Midland 65 million. Now, such a levy would raise some two billion pounds.
"Banks were making a lot of money and you've got to remember that there was much less competition and that things like interest-bearing current accounts didn't exist," said one banker.
So, banks could take in deposits and would be lending at huge interest rates and making big profits.
Lawson decided that a levy on non-interest bearing deposits was the best way to get some of the money back.

The cash went to the Treasury, another major difference to today's circumstances where Brown has earmarked the proceeds of his windfall tax on the utilities to fund a programme to reduce unemployment.

Another big difference between the two taxes is that the current Labour government has an electoral mandate to raise the money by taxing utilities though it was not specific about which companies would be selected.
The Conservative government of 1981 had no mandate to tax the banks but got round that by claiming exceptional circumstances.

In 1981, all the banks "suffered" but building societies, which then were not in such direct competition, did not. This echoes the argument of companies like British Telecommunications in 1997 which say that if they are taxed it will be unfair because it will aid their competitors.
No one expects the Labour government to tax banks now even though they are making big profits again -- 12.6 billion pounds for the six London-based banks.
